cover.headline: A trusted franchise, with a costly new bet and a full price
cover.lead: Urban Company is India's largest online home-services platform: 9.3 million customers booked beauty, cleaning and repair jobs from ~79,000 trained partners in the year to Jun-2026. The core is accelerating (India services NTV +29% in Q1FY27 at a 6.9% margin) and International and Native are profitable or close. But InstaHelp, its on-demand house-help service, lost ₹132 cr in the quarter, twice what the core earned. The stock trades at ₹{{P.last|num}}, 53% above the ₹103 IPO price, and ~3.34x next year's core NTV against a median of 3.05x since November. Our sum of the parts gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}})**: **we initiate with SELL.** Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}} ({{scen.bear.upside|chg}}). The street's median target is ₹152.5.

arguments.h: The core is a quality business, and it is accelerating
arguments.p: India services NTV grew 29% in Q1FY27, the fourth quarter of acceleration, at a 6.9% of NTV margin (+170 bp). International (+76% NTV) and Native are profitable or close to it. Together the core earned ₹67 cr of adjusted EBITDA in one quarter, against ₹106 cr in all of FY26.

arguments.h: InstaHelp is a subsidy war that will run for years
arguments.p: The house-help service lost ₹132 cr in Q1FY27, twice what the core earned, at ₹346 an order, against venture-funded Snabbit and Pronto. Management needs pricing to rise from ~₹150 to ~₹200 an hour and says that could take up to five years. We forecast losses of ₹380-560 cr a year to FY29E and value them at −₹1,003 cr.

₹2,019 cr of cash and no debt mean no new money is needed on our numbers. But venture funds still own ~40% and have sold into every rally since the Mar-2026 lock-in expiry; SBI Mutual Fund has been the buyer.

arguments.h: Valuation: the price already assumes the good outcome
arguments.p: At ₹157 the market pays 3.34x next year's core NTV, against a median of 3.05x since Nov-2025, while internet stocks de-rated −11.8% over the same months. At our derived 2.7x Sep-28E core NTV, less InstaHelp losses, the sum of the parts gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): SELL. The street's median target is ₹152.5.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): does India services growth hold above 25% against a tougher base, and does the InstaHelp loss stop rising?
InstaHelp pricing and rivals: average order value (₹138) and loss per order (₹346); Snabbit and Pronto fund-raising.
Supply: venture funds still hold ~40%; block sales by Accel, VY Capital and Bessemer have met every rally.
Guidance test: group adjusted EBITDA breakeven by Q3FY28 needs the InstaHelp loss to roughly halve within 18 months.

sections.title: A managed marketplace for jobs inside the home

blocks.p: Urban Company runs an app on which households book services at home: beauty and spa, cleaning and pest control, electricians, plumbers, carpenters, appliance repair and painting. It is a **full-stack** (managed) marketplace: it does not just list providers but trains them, sells them tools and consumables, sets prices, checks quality through ratings and stands behind the job. Partners are independent; Urban Company keeps a commission plus fees (its "take rate"). It also sells its own **Native** water purifiers and smart locks, runs the same model in the **UAE and Singapore** (and Saudi Arabia through a JV), and since 2025 offers **InstaHelp**, on-demand house help. Its headline measure is **NTV**, what customers pay for services and Native products.

blocks.callout: **Two numbers matter most.** The India-services margin (adjusted EBITDA as a % of NTV) shows whether the core is turning scale into profit: 4.1% in FY26, 6.9% in Q1FY27 (seasonally strong), target 9-10%. The InstaHelp loss shows how much of that profit is being reinvested: ₹132 cr in Q1FY27. The group breaks even when the first outgrows the second.

sections.title: Eleven years to build trust in the home; a profitable core by FY26

blocks.p: Urban Company was set up in 2014 as UrbanClap, a marketplace that connected customers with local service providers. It found that listing providers was not enough: customers wanted a guaranteed standard. So it moved to a "full-stack" model in which it trains, equips, prices and rates its partners and stands behind the job. That model took a decade and ~₹1,400 cr of venture money in FY22 alone to scale, but by FY24 the India business was close to breakeven. Three recent events shape today's numbers: the 2025 launch of InstaHelp (a costly new category), the Sep-2025 IPO, and the Mar-2026 end of the pre-IPO lock-in.

The bigger cost to shareholders today is supply: the six-month lock-in ended on 17-Mar-2026, freeing ~66% of the shares, and venture funds have been sellers since.

sections.title: A huge market that is still 99% offline; the only online rivals of size are in house help

blocks.p: India's home-services market is large but almost entirely offline: Redseer (in the IPO prospectus) puts it at US$59 bn in CY2024, growing 10-11% a year to ~US$97 bn by CY2029, with online platforms under 1% of it. Brokers' estimates are similar: ₹5.1-5.2 lakh crore in FY25 rising to ₹8.4-8.6 lakh crore by FY30, online share 0.8% → 1.3% (Ambit, Mar-2026); online full-stack home services ₹4,100-4,300 cr in FY25, growing 18-22% a year, of which Urban Company has ~65-70% (MOSL, Mar-2026).

In its core categories Urban Company has no listed or scaled online rival: competition is the local beautician, electrician or cleaner found by word of mouth, plus NoBroker's home services (~2 lakh requests a month, Zivora beauty brand). InstaHelp is different: on-demand house help has drawn venture money. Snabbit raised US$56 mn in Apr-2026 (valued ~US$350 mn) and ran ~1.85 mn orders in Jul-2026; Pronto raised US$45 mn at a ~US$200 mn valuation by May-2026 (~0.95 mn orders a month). InstaHelp is the largest, with >100,000 daily orders by Aug-2026, but all three subsidise orders.

sections.title: The core: growth accelerating to 29%, margin at 6.9% of NTV and rising

blocks.p: India consumer services (excluding InstaHelp) is 74% of group NTV and the source of nearly all profit. Customers book a job (a facial, a deep clean, an AC repair) at a fixed price; a trained partner arrives with Urban Company's tools and products; Urban Company keeps ~34% of what the customer pays as commission, fees and product sales to the partner. NTV grew 29% in Q1FY27 to ₹1,056 cr: users +21% to 8.2 mn, spend per user +7%. Growth has accelerated for four quarters (10% → 19% → 21% → 26% → 29%), partly because Q1FY26 was hit by unseasonal rain.

blocks.p: **How the margin keeps rising.** The +170 bp YoY in Q1FY27 came in equal parts from contribution margin (AI tools cut customer and partner support costs) and operating leverage (revenue grew faster than salaries and overheads). Partners work more hours as density rises (59 a month in FY22, 90 in FY26), which raises their earnings and cuts churn and onboarding costs. Management targets 9-10% of NTV "over the next few years" and says it will not "squeeze all the margins out overnight". We assume ~120 bp a year: 5.6% / 6.8% / 7.8% for FY27-29E.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** this is a good business: a decade of operating data, a trusted brand and density that rivals cannot buy quickly. Growth near 20% and margins rising toward 9-10% of NTV are credible. The risks are the partners (pay, social-security rules, protests) and disintermediation (customers rebooking the same partner offline).

sections.title: International is a second profit engine; Native is close to breakeven

blocks.p: **International** (UAE and Singapore, wholly owned) runs the India playbook for local customers and the diaspora. NTV grew 75% in FY26 (ex-KSA) to ₹700 cr and 76% in Q1FY27 (58% in constant currency); adjusted EBITDA turned positive in FY26 (₹6 cr) and was ₹3 cr in Q1FY27. The Middle East conflict cut UAE demand 15-20% in late March 2026, without a lasting fall in frequency. In Saudi Arabia Urban Company runs **Yammak**, a 50:50 JV with SMASCO: NTV ₹77 cr in Q1FY27 (+135%), loss narrowing to ₹9 cr (100% basis).

**Native** sells Urban Company's own water purifiers (sold with long service plans) and electronic door locks, on the app, on marketplaces and in stores. NTV grew 122% in FY26 to ₹345 cr and 51% in Q1FY27; the loss narrowed from −25.1% of NTV (FY25) to −8.9% (FY26) and −7.3% (Q1FY27). More than half of FY26 purifier buyers were new to Urban Company. Management targets a ₹1,000 cr revenue business and sees profit "over the next few quarters"; the weaker rupee and commodity prices are a near-term cost headwind.

We forecast International NTV +50% / 35% / 28% at margins rising to 4.5% of NTV, and Native +45% / 35% / 30%, breaking even in FY28E. Together they add ₹{{dcf.sotp.parts.1.perShare|n1}} and ₹{{dcf.sotp.parts.2.perShare|n1}} a share to our sum of the parts.

sections.title: InstaHelp: from 72,000 to 3.8 mn orders a quarter, at a loss of ₹346 an order

blocks.p: InstaHelp sends a house-help professional on demand for daily cleaning and housekeeping, booked by the hour. It started in 2025 and grew from 72,000 orders in Q1FY26 to 3.8 mn in Q1FY27. It is the most frequent service Urban Company offers: weekly or daily, against monthly or quarterly for the core. But it is in a price war: the average order fell from ₹172 (Q3FY26) to ₹138, venture-funded Snabbit and Pronto subsidise orders too, and InstaHelp lost ₹132 cr in Q1FY27 (₹235 cr in FY26). Management says the category needs ~₹200 an hour to break even (~₹150 covers only the partner and gross costs) and that getting there could take "a couple of years" or, in the worst case, five.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** we value InstaHelp at the present value of the losses still to fund after Mar-2027 (−₹1,003 cr, ~₹6 a share; factor 2.1 on our FY28E loss), not at an option value. The strategic case is real (frequency, a "volume moat" around the core), and it could become valuable if rivals run out of money. But today each order loses more than twice what it brings in, and the street's positive values for InstaHelp (Emkay ₹28 a share, MOSL ₹10) assume an outcome that is not yet visible.

blocks.callout: **Verdict: a narrow but real moat in the core.** In beauty, cleaning and repairs, no online rival of size has emerged in a decade: the hard part (training, quality control, local density, trust inside the home) is what Urban Company has built. The moat is weaker against the informal market (customers can rebook a partner directly) and in InstaHelp, where the product is simpler and venture money can buy share. Pricing power exists in premium beauty, less so elsewhere.

sections.title: Revenue up 7x in six years; the core now makes money, InstaHelp spends it

blocks.p: Urban Company's revenue rose from ₹219 cr in FY20 to ₹1,556 cr in FY26 (+36% in FY26). Revenue is the company's share of what customers pay (commission and fees), plus products it sells to its service partners and Native's water purifiers and locks; it is ~36% of the value customers spend on the platform (NTV, ₹4,290 cr in FY26). The loss peaked at ₹514 cr in FY22, fell to ₹93 cr in FY24, and FY25 showed a ₹240 cr profit only because of a ₹211 cr one-time tax credit. In FY26 the loss was back at ₹235 cr: the core businesses earned ₹106 cr of adjusted EBITDA, but the new InstaHelp house-help service lost ₹235 cr and ₹60 cr of deferred-tax assets were written back.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** read Urban Company in two halves. The core (India services, International, Native) is profitable and its margin is rising: adjusted EBITDA went from ₹12 cr in FY25 to ₹106 cr in FY26 and ₹67 cr in Q1FY27 alone. InstaHelp is a start-up inside a listed company, losing more than the core earns. Group EBITDA as reported (Screener −₹254 cr in FY26) also carries ESOP cost (₹104 cr) and the Saudi JV loss (₹31 cr). Treasury income (₹137 cr) covers about half of the loss.

sections.title: Reported vs adjusted: rent, ESOPs, the Saudi JV and tax credits

blocks.p: Urban Company's headline profit measure, **adjusted EBITDA**, is the sum of its four segment results. It is stricter than most on one point (it deducts rent, ₹38 cr in FY26) and looser on others (it leaves out ESOP cost, one-offs and the loss of the Saudi JV). In FY26 adjusted EBITDA was −₹129 cr; adding back rent and deducting ESOP (₹104 cr) and one-offs (₹28 cr of listing costs and a warehouse fire) gives Ind AS EBITDA of −₹223 cr. After depreciation (₹45 cr), the JV loss (₹31 cr), lease interest (₹12 cr) and treasury income (₹137 cr), the pre-tax loss was ₹175 cr; a ₹60 cr tax charge (deferred-tax assets written back) took the net loss to ₹235 cr.

pair.title: FY26: from adjusted EBITDA to net loss
pair.source: Q4FY26 letter (reconciliations, pp. 23-26)

pair.title: ESOP cost is rising after the IPO grants
pair.source: Urban Company shareholders' letters and FY26 annual report, GAM Research

bullets: **FY25 was not a real profit.** The ₹240 cr net profit included a ₹211 cr one-time deferred-tax credit; PBT was ₹29 cr. In FY26 ₹60 cr of those assets were written back because some tax losses may lapse while InstaHelp keeps the group loss-making, and ₹151 cr remain on the standalone balance sheet.

**ESOP is a real cost.** 10.0 cr options (~6.4% of the company) were outstanding at Mar-26 at ₹1. We count them in the share count (156.2 cr) and charge ₹150-170 cr a year in our forecasts (₹38 cr in Q1FY27).
**Treasury income props up the bottom line.** ₹131 cr of interest on bonds and deposits in FY26 covered half of the operating loss; it shrinks as cash funds InstaHelp.

**Two "EBITDA"s.** Screener's FY26 EBITDA (−₹254 cr) includes the ₹31 cr Saudi JV loss; the company's Ind AS EBITDA (−₹223 cr) does not. Our model follows Screener's definition for history and forecasts.
**Tax is paid even in a loss.** Profitable subsidiaries paid ₹8 cr of tax in Q1FY27. Our model taxes only positive group profit, so FY27-28E losses are slightly understated.
**Contingent liabilities are modest:** ₹116 cr, mainly GST demands (₹52 cr paid under protest).

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** Disclosure is excellent: segment P&Ls, a reconciliation to Ind AS and free cash flow every quarter, and the auditor's report is clean. But ESOP cost, a JV loss outside adjusted EBITDA, and tax credits that came and went make the headline numbers easy to misread.

sections.title: Cash: ₹2,019 cr, no debt, customers pay up front

blocks.p: Urban Company held ₹2,019 cr of cash, deposits and treasury investments at Jun-2026 (company figure) and has no borrowings: the ₹136 cr of "borrowings" on Screener are lease liabilities on offices and training centres. The IPO brought in ₹469 cr net in Sep-2025. Working capital is negative: customers pay when they book, while partners and suppliers are paid later, so growth releases a little cash; Native's inventory (₹90 cr at Mar-26) is the main use. Screener's "cash + investments" (₹1,794 cr at Mar-26) is lower than the company figure because ₹227 cr of deposits sit inside other assets.

sections.title: Ownership: venture funds selling, SBI Mutual Fund buying

blocks.p: The three founders are the promoters, with 6.34% each (19.0% together). The rest of the register is mostly the venture and growth funds that financed the company before the IPO. Because most of them are foreign entities, they sit in the "FII" bucket, which is why foreign holdings look so high (55% at Jun-2026). The six-month lock-in on pre-IPO holders ended on 17-Mar-2026; since then SBI Mutual Fund has been the main buyer and venture funds the main sellers.

blocks.p: The street is split almost evenly. The bulls (UBS, Emkay, Morgan Stanley, Kotak, Ventura) argue that Urban Company is the only scaled, trusted online brand in a market less than 1% online, that core margins are heading to the 9-10% of NTV target, and that InstaHelp can become a frequency engine (UBS calls it a "Blinkit moment" for home services). The sceptics (Ambit, JM Financial, BofA) say the core grows ~18-20% a year rather than 30%, InstaHelp has poor unit economics against well-funded rivals, and the price already pays 45-60x FY28E EBITDA for the core. Most brokers use a sum of the parts with the core on EV/EBITDA (JM 45x, MOSL 50x, Emkay ~57x FY28E); Goldman Sachs and Ambit lean on a DCF. The LSEG median was ₹145 (9 brokers) on 26-Aug-2026; our table of 10 gives ₹152.5.

sections.title: Valuation: sum of the parts on order value gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}

blocks.h: How the street values Urban Company

blocks.p: Urban Company makes a loss, so P/E is no use. Brokers value it as a sum of the parts: the core on EV/EBITDA two years out, Native and International on sales, InstaHelp on NTV or at nil; Goldman Sachs and Ambit use a DCF. We keep the sum of the parts, but value the core on EV/NTV, the one yardstick we can derive from the stock's own trading (EBITDA is too small and too volatile a base), deduct the present value of InstaHelp's losses to breakeven (our house rule for start-up losses), and add the cash. A DCF and Goldman Sachs' EV/sales are cross-checks.

blocks.h: Our core multiple: 2.7x NTV, and why

blocks.p: Urban Company listed on 17-Sep-2025 at a 57% premium to its ₹103 issue price, so its own history is short. Following our rule for recent listings (HYUNDAI, HDBFS, MEESHO), we skip the IPO-premium months: September (median 4.51x forward core NTV, peak 4.96x) and October (4.11x), until the anchor lock-in expiry, the first broker initiations and the first results as a listed company. We use every daily close from 1-Nov-2025 to 30-Sep-2026: 226 closes, eleven months rather than twelve. We pair it with the sector's move over the same window.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a good core, an expensive experiment, a full price

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's only scaled, trusted online home-services brand, with a core that grows ~20-30% and earns rising margins (India services 6.9% of NTV in Q1FY27), profitable international operations, a Native products arm near breakeven, ₹2,019 cr of cash and no debt. Our sum of the parts gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}).

**What you are paying for:** ~₹24,600 cr of market value. With InstaHelp at the present value of its losses (−₹1,003 cr), the price implies ~3.15x our Sep-28E core NTV, above the stock's own median (3.05x) and our 2.7x, at a time when internet stocks have de-rated. To justify it, either India services must reach its 9-10% margin target sooner while growing 25%+, or InstaHelp must turn from a ₹500 cr-a-year cost into a valuable business. Both are possible; neither is in our base case.
